title: Short side and long side
summary: When Philidor is no longer possible: rook behind the pawn, king to the short side and checks from the long side.
key.behind: The black king has already passed the third rank, so Philidor's defence no longer works. The only way out is to bring the white rook behind the pawn.
key.tarrasch: Tarrasch, 1906: the white king on the short side, the rook on the long side, far from the pawn, checking from the side. A draw.
key.close: The same idea with the rook one file closer to the pawn: now it loses. For side checks to work, the rook needs at least three files of distance.
part.behind.title: Rook behind the pawn
part.behind.summary: When the third rank no longer works, the rook goes behind the pawn and ties it to its king.
step.t_behind: The black king has reached f3, and the third rank is no longer any use to your rook. What holds the pawn now?
step.t_behind.hint1: The pawn only moves if its king comes along. From where does your rook bother every step it takes?
step.t_behind.hint2: Look at the pawn's file, far from it.
step.behind: The rook goes behind the pawn, to e8. From there it attacks the pawn at every step, always along the same file. The pawn only advances with the black king glued to it: on its own, it falls.
step.d_late: First, see what happens if the rook insists on the third rank and checks on b3. You watch from Black's side, who is now to move.
step.d_late.m1: The pawn blocks the check and advances for free: the white rook has left the e-file, and nothing attacks the pawn from behind.
step.d_late.m2: The white rook attacks the pawn from the side, but the black king protects it.
step.d_late.m3: Check on the first rank. The white king has no square: e2 and f2 belong to the black king, d2 to the pawn. The rook has to block.
step.d_late.m4: The rook is back on the first rank, but as a shield, not to give checks.
step.d_late.m5: Black trades rooks. Without them, all that counts is who reaches the queening square first.
step.d_late.m6: The white king recaptures, but it is on the wrong side of the pawn.
step.d_late.m7: The black king takes e1 and e2, and the pawn runs all the way. That is why the rook had to go to e8.
step.behindPawn: Now you. From where does your rook hold the pawn?
step.behindPawn.hint: On the pawn's file, as far from it as possible.
step.behindPawn.done: With the rook on e8, the pawn does not move on its own. But the black king comes to e3 and threatens 2...Ra1, mate: your king will have to leave the queening square. Which way is the next chapter.
part.short.title: The short side
part.short.summary: The pawn splits the board in two: the king takes the short side, the rook the long side.
step.t_short: A bishop's pawn now. Your rook is already behind it, but the black king on f3 threatens 1...Ra1, mate. Which way does your king go?
step.t_short.hint1: Count the files on each side of the pawn.
step.t_short.hint2: Soon your rook will want to give side checks. On which side does it have more room?
step.sides: The pawn on f splits the board. To its right there are two files, g and h: the short side. To its left, five, from a to e: the long side. The king goes to the short side, 1.Kg1, and leaves the whole long side to the rook. King on the short side, rook on the long side: that is Karstedt's method.
step.d_arkell1: A real game: Chris Ward against Keith Arkell, British Championship, Norwich, 1994. After many trades, the white king has just captured the pawn on f6, and Black can no longer reach the Philidor defence. Arkell defends as in this lesson. You watch from his side.
step.d_arkell1.m1: The rook goes behind the pawn, as in the first chapter. From f4 it attacks the pawn, and the white king has to stay glued to it.
step.d_arkell1.m2: Check: White wants to push the black king away from the front of the pawn.
step.d_arkell1.m3: The only square, and on the right side: g and h are the short side of the f-pawn. The long side is left to the black rook.
step.d_arkell1.m4: The white king steps away from the front of the pawn to push it forward.
step.d_arkell1.m5: The black king comes straight back near the queening square, which is free again.
step.d_arkell1.m6: Another check, to push the black king away again.
step.d_arkell1.m7: The king goes to f8, in front of the pawn: the best square it has.
step.d_arkell1.m8: The white king returns to f6, taking e7 and g7.
step.d_arkell1.m9: The black king stays on g8, on the short side, and the rook is still behind the pawn. Five moves later, White has not advanced a step.
step.d_blunder: Now the mistake, back with the bishop's pawn. The white king went to e1, the long side, and
step.d_blunder.m1: Check. With the king on e1, the only square is d2: the king runs even further to the long side.
step.d_blunder.m2: The white king is now on the long side, far from the pawn.
step.d_blunder.m3: The black rook takes the queening square, f1. With it there, the black king can step away from the front of the pawn.
step.d_blunder.m4: The white rook looks for a place to give side checks. On the long side it runs into its own king; on the short side, g and h, it has no distance.
step.d_blunder.m5: The black king steps out of the pawn's way, on the short side, and clears its path.
step.d_blunder.m6: Check, but from close range: on the short side the rook has no distance, and the black king just steps back in front of the pawn.
step.d_blunder.m7: The black king returns to f2 and takes e1, e2 and e3. The white king can no longer reach the pawn: Black wins.
step.shortRook: The black rook is on h2, right on the short side. It threatens 1...Rh1+: your rook would have to block on g1, and the trade gives Black a won pawn ending. Where does your king go?
step.shortRook.hint: The short side is still the king's, and it can arrive with an attack.
step.shortRook.done: 1.Kg1 attacks the rook: it has to leave, and you have gained a tempo. The king went to the short side even with the black rook there. That is what Karstedt showed in 1897.
part.lateral.title: Side checks
part.lateral.summary: With the pawn one step from queening, the rook on the long side gives side checks until the black king lets go of the pawn.
step.t_tarrasch: Now the pawn is already on e2, one step from queening, and the black king on e1, in front of it. Your king is on the short side, your rook on the other side. Can you still hold?
step.t_tarrasch.hint1: Your rook is far from the pawn. Is that good or bad?
step.t_tarrasch.hint2: For the pawn to queen, the black king must leave e1. What does the rook do each time it moves?
step.lateral: This position is Siegbert Tarrasch's, from 1906. The black king is stuck on e1: for the pawn to queen it has to get out, and it cannot go to f1 or f2, which belong to your king. On the other side, the rook is waiting with side checks from far away.
step.d_checks: The first checks, one at a time.
step.d_checks.m1: Check. The black king cannot go to f1 or f2: it goes to d2.
step.d_checks.m2: The king has left e1, but the pawn still cannot queen: the rook on a1 watches e1.
step.d_checks.m3: The check continues along the second rank. Black has to answer it, and there is no time to queen.
step.d_checks.m4: The king climbs to escape the checks, and stays one step from the pawn.
step.d_checks.m5: Another check on the same a-file. The rook is far away, and the black king cannot reach it.
step.d_checks.m6: The king keeps running, and now the pawn on e2 has no king beside it.
step.checks: Carry on. While the black king is near the pawn, check from the side; when it moves away, the rook attacks the pawn.
step.checks.hint: Keep checking along the a-file. When the black king lets go of the pawn, the rook goes to the e-file, behind it.
step.checks.done: The black king walked to the b-file to escape the checks, and the rook went behind the pawn. A draw.
part.flank.title: Karstedt's manoeuvre
part.flank.summary: When the attacking rook screens the pawn from the front, yours goes to the most distant file.
step.t_karstedt: The black rook has gone to e1, in front of the pawn and the king. It looks after the queening square, and the black king is now free to step away from the front of the pawn. Where does your rook work best now?
step.t_karstedt.hint1: Once free, the black king will step away from the pawn. What will you want to do at that moment?
step.t_karstedt.hint2: To give side checks, the rook needs distance.
step.t_karstedt.hint3: A rook checking from far away cannot be reached by the king unless it abandons the pawn.
step.karstedt: This is the moment Max Karstedt discovered in 1897. Before him, Johann Berger considered this defence lost. Karstedt saw that, when the attacking rook screens the pawn from the front, the defending rook goes to the file furthest from the pawn, the a-file, and from there threatens side checks. Three files lie between it and the pawn, and the black king cannot reach it without abandoning the pawn.
step.d_karstedt.m1: The rook goes to a8. If the black king steps away from the front of the pawn, the side checks come, from far away.
step.d_karstedt.m2: Black prepares a shield: from d1, the rook can step into the path of the side checks. But to do it, it has left the e-file.
step.d_karstedt.m3: So your rook goes back behind the pawn and attacks it. Only the king protects it now, and the king is tied down again.
step.d_karstedt.m4: The black rook protects the pawn from the side, to free the king once more.
step.d_karstedt.m5: Your king returns next to the queening square, on the short side, and watches e1 and e2.
step.d_karstedt.m6: The black king tries another route, via d2.
step.d_karstedt.m7: Your king follows, to f2, eyeing the queening square. Rook behind the pawn, king on the short side: Black makes no progress.
step.d_arkell2: Ward against Arkell again, six moves later. White has just put the rook on f8, in front of the pawn, to free the king. It is Karstedt's moment, and Arkell recognised it.
step.d_arkell2.m1: Arkell takes the rook to a4, on the long side: four files lie between it and the pawn. The side checks are ready.
step.d_arkell2.m2: Check: White pushes the black king.
step.d_arkell2.m3: The king stays on the short side, on g8, next to the queening square.
step.d_arkell2.m4: White moves the rook out of the way and looks for another plan.
step.d_arkell2.m5: The black king returns in front of the pawn, to f8.
step.d_arkell2.m6: The white rook goes to e6, to shield the king from checks along the sixth rank.
step.d_arkell2.m7: The black rook moves to the seventh, still on the a-file, and waits for the next check. The game was drawn on move 57.
step.flankNow: A queen's pawn now, and it has already reached the third rank. The black rook is on d1, in front of the pawn and the king. Your king is on the short side. Can you wait one more move?
step.flankNow.hint: Your king is to the left of the pawn. The rook goes to the other side, as far away as it can.
step.flankNow.done: 1.Rh8: three files lie between the rook and the pawn, and the first side check has already come. With the pawn on the third, the time is now: it is the only move that holds.
part.distance.title: Three files
part.distance.summary: With the rook too close, the attacking king walks up to it and the checks run out.
step.t_close: Tarrasch's position, with your rook one file closer, on b7. Do the checks still save you?
step.t_close.hint1: Follow the checks and see where the black king ends up.
step.t_close.hint2: What happens when the black king comes up against your rook?
step.distance: They do not. From b, the rook has only two files to the pawn, c and d. The black king escapes the checks by walking toward it, and reaches it in a few steps. That is why the rule is three files between the rook and the pawn, and why the king goes to the short side: so the rook keeps the whole long side.
step.d_close: Watch from Black's side, who is now attacking.
step.d_close.m1: The same first check as in Tarrasch's position.
step.d_close.m2: The king goes to d2, its only square.
step.d_close.m3: Check along the second rank, as before.
step.d_close.m4: The king climbs, still beside the pawn.
step.d_close.m5: Another check, but from close range now: only c3 lies between the rook and the black king.
step.d_close.m6: The black king walks toward the rook and attacks it. It has to leave, and the checks are over.
step.d_close.m7: The white rook goes behind the pawn, but the black king is one step from it.
step.d_close.m8: The king returns to d2, protects the pawn and takes e1. The pawn will queen.
step.closeWin: Now you attack, with Black. The white rook is too close. Escape the checks.
step.closeWin.hint: Walk toward the rook, without moving away from the pawn.
step.closeWin.done: With only two files, the king reached the rook and got back to the pawn in time.
part.block.title: The rook trade
part.block.summary: Before trading rooks, count the pawn ending. If it loses, the rook waits on the first rank.
step.t_block: Now the black rook joins in. The pawn is on the third and the black king on e2. Your king is on the short side, your rook far away on the a-file. What do you play?
step.t_block.hint1: Start with the move that gives Black no time.
step.t_block.hint2: And if the black rook blocks the check, do you trade?
step.block: 1.Ra2+, and the black rook blocks on d2. Trading looks natural, but count first: after 2.Rxd2+ Kxd2, the black king stands beside the pawn and takes e1, and your king on g2 is too late. That pawn ending is lost. The rook does not trade: it goes back to the first rank and waits.
step.d_trade: See from Black's side what happens if you trade the rooks.
step.d_trade.m1: The trade looks like relief, but it removes the only piece watching the first rank.
step.d_trade.m2: The black king captures and stands right beside the pawn, guarding e1.
step.d_trade.m3: Your king attacks the pawn, but the black king protects it: you cannot capture.
step.d_trade.m4: The pawn reaches the second rank, still protected, and only e1 is left.
step.d_trade.m5: Your king eyes e1, but cannot go there: the black king on d2 guards that square too.
step.d_trade.m6: The pawn queens with check. That is why the rook does not trade: it goes back to the first rank and waits.
step.blockE: Now you, in the same position. Do not trade: wait on the first rank and bring the king.
step.blockE.hint: The rook goes back to the first rank; after the check, your king comes via f3 to attack the pawn.
step.blockE.done: The black king was guarding the pawn, but so was your king on f3: the rook captured it, and the black king cannot recapture. A draw.
part.carlsen.title: Aronian versus Carlsen
part.carlsen.summary: Not every moment calls for a check: with the rook already in place, the right move can be a king move.
step.t_carlsen: Moscow, 2006: it is your turn to play as Carlsen, with Black. Your rook is already on the a-file, on the long side, and your king is on the short side. Check, or something else?
step.t_carlsen.hint1: If you check on a7, where does the white king go? Does it still get checked there?
step.t_carlsen.hint2: The rook is fine where it is. Look for a move that waits without letting go of f7.
step.carlsen: Levon Aronian against Magnus Carlsen, Tal Memorial, Moscow, 2006, round six. Carlsen was defending with his rook on the long side, as Karstedt prescribes, and after 71.e6 Ra7+ 72.Rd7 Ra8 73.Rd6 they reached this position. He played 73...Ra7+, the white king went to e8, and Carlsen resigned.
step.d_carlsenError: Why Carlsen resigned: watch from Aronian's side.
step.d_carlsenError.m1: The next check, along the eighth rank.
step.d_carlsenError.m2: The white rook blocks on d8. The king on e8 is sheltered in front of the pawn, and the checks are over.
step.d_carlsenError.m3: The black rook attacks the pawn along the sixth rank.
step.d_carlsenError.m4: The pawn steps out of the attack and reaches the seventh, with the king in front and the rook dealing with the checks. White wins: that is what Carlsen saw.
step.king: Now play the move that saved the game. The rook stays where it is.
step.king.hint: The king keeps an eye on f7 without stepping onto the eighth rank.
step.king.done: 73...Kg6 was the only move. On g8 the king walks into 74.Rd8+ and the trade of rooks; on h6, h7 or h8 the white king goes to f7; any rook move lets the white king shelter on e8 or the rook block on d8. Then the king came back to the pawn and the rook kept checking: a draw.
step.recap: Three rules to take to your games. One: if the third rank no longer works, the rook goes behind the pawn. Two: when the king has to leave, it goes to the short side, and the long side is left to the rook. Three: when the attacking rook screens the pawn from the front, yours goes to the most distant file, three files from the pawn, and checks from the side. And if the black rook blocks the check, count the pawn ending before you trade.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge: rook behind the pawn, king to the short side and, if the pawn advances, checks from the side.
key.karstedt: Max Karstedt's manoeuvre (Deutsches Wochenschach, 1897), with colours reversed: the attacking rook has screened the pawn from the front, and the defending one goes to the a-file.
key.arkell: Ward against Arkell, British Championship, Norwich, 1994: Black could not reach the Philidor defence and drew with 45...Rf4!, the rook behind the pawn.
key.carlsen: Aronian vs Carlsen, 2006: here only a king move drew. Carlsen checked with the rook and lost.
history: When Philidor's defence is no longer possible, there is still a way out: the king runs to the short side of the pawn, the side with fewer files, and the rook goes to the long side to check from a distance. The manuals of the nineteenth century gave these endings up as lost, and Johann Berger was still saying so in 1890. In 1897 the German teacher Max Karstedt showed otherwise: the position is a draw, as long as king and rook are on the right sides. Siegbert Tarrasch studied the same ending in 1906, and the side-check positions in this lesson are his. In practice the defence is still hard: in 2006 a young Magnus Carlsen lost a drawn position to Levon Aronian because he gave a check when the right move was a king move.
practice: Practical challenge: the black king is already in and Philidor is no longer possible. Rook behind the pawn, king to the short side and, if the pawn advances, side checks. The goal is to draw.
ex.e11: This is the starting point of Max Karstedt's manoeuvre, from 1897. The black king threatens mate on the first rank, and the black rook is on h2, right on the short side. Where does your king go? Find the draw.
ex.e11.hint: The black rook on the short side doesn't change the rule. Think about who will need the long side in a moment.
ex.e11.solution: 1.Kf1! The king goes to the short side, even with the black rook there. After 1...Rh1+, 2.Kg2 attacks the rook, and the long side stays free for your rook to give checks. 1.Kd1 loses: the king would stand in its own rook's way. Berger, in 1890, thought this position was lost; Karstedt showed the draw.
ex.e13: Now you attack. Tarrasch's position, 1906: the black king is on the short side, but the black rook is too close to the pawn. Escape the checks. Find the winning move.
ex.e13.hint: There are only two files between the black rook and the pawn. Walk the king toward the rook without abandoning the pawn.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Kc7, the only move. After 1...Ra7+, 2.Kc8 (2.Kc6, 2.Kd6 and 2.Kd8 also win); on 2...Ra8+, 3.Kb7 (or 3.Kc7), and when the black rook goes behind the pawn, 3...Rd8, 4.Kc7 protects the pawn and it queens. The black rook needed three files of distance: with two, the white king reaches it and gets back to the pawn in time.
ex.e09: The black king stands beside the pawn, and its rook on c2 closes the second rank to your checks. Find the defence.
ex.e09.hint: Trading rooks leads to a pawn ending: count it before you accept. If it loses, the rook has another rank to watch, and your king needs to get close to the pawn.
ex.e09.solution: 1.Ra1! Trading, 1.Rxc2+? Kxc2, loses: the black king stays glued to the pawn, and yours never reaches e1. From the first rank the rook watches the queening square and threatens checks again. After 1...e3 2.Kf3 e2 3.Kf2 the king closes in on the pawn; when 3...Rb2 lets go of the e-file, 4.Re1 blocks the pawn, protected by the king, and after 4...Kd3 the rook returns with 5.Ra1 to threaten checks once more.
ex.e10: The black king slipped away to e2, next to yours, and the black rook is already on b1, on the first rank. Your rook stands in front of the pawn, doing nothing. Find the plan.
ex.e10.hint: First a check, to drive the black king away from yours. Then the rook looks for the file furthest from the pawn: from there, every step of the pawn meets a side check.
ex.e10.solution: 1.Rf2+ Kd3 2.Ra2 e3 3.Ra3+ Kd2 4.Ra2+. After the check the rook takes the a-file, the farthest one, and the side checks hold. If the black rook steps in front of a check, on b2 or b3, the black king does not protect it and your rook captures it. 1.Ra8 also draws.
ex.e14: A bishop's pawn on the other wing: your king is on the short side, on b1, and the black rook has just attacked yours. Where does it go? Find the draw.
ex.e14.hint: Neither capture nor attack the pawn: any quiet move gives Black 1...c2+ and the pawn queens. Your rook is far from the pawn. Use the distance, as Tarrasch did.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Rh2+! The side check comes from far away: four files lie between the rook and the pawn, and the black king cannot reach it without abandoning the pawn. After 1...Kd3, 2.Rh3+ repeats the idea, and Black never finds time for the pawn's step to c2. 1.Rxf5? and 1.Rh3? lose to 1...c2+ followed by 2...c1=Q, and any other rook move allows 1...c2+ too.
